The Variance Matrix of a Fit

Source: R/inference.R
vcov.StatmodFit.Rd

Returns the variance of the estimated coefficients, over every distribution parameter's block at once.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'StatmodFit'
vcov(
  object,
  type = c("bayesian", "frequentist", "unconditional"),
  expected = NULL,
  approx = c("opg", "bartlett", "integrate", "mc"),
  readable = TRUE,
  parameter = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

object

A StatmodFit().

type

"bayesian", "frequentist" or "unconditional". The first two are conditional on the hyperparameters; the third carries their own uncertainty as well.

expected

Whether the expected information is used. Defaults to fit_expected(), which selects the expected information where the fit inverted it and the family writes it out, and the observed Hessian otherwise. A model that carries a structural term always uses the observed information.

approx

How the expected information is approximated for a family with no closed form: "opg" (the default), "bartlett", "integrate" or "mc". Read only when expected is TRUE and the family has no closed form.

readable

Whether the matrix is over the quantities that the model reports (TRUE, the default) or over the coordinates on which it was estimated (FALSE). A structural term declares its quantities, for example a persistence, and their variance is obtained by the delta method.

parameter

The distribution parameters whose rows and columns are kept. NULL keeps all of them.

...

Unused.

Value

A square matrix with dimnames parameter:name. By default it is over the quantities that the model reports, which include the own parameters of a structural term. With readable = FALSE it is over the coefficients of every equation, the free parameters of a structural term following those of its own equation. parameter restricts it to the rows and columns of the named equations. A coordinate that is held or not identified has NA in its row and column.

Details

Writing \(H\) for the information of the log-likelihood and \(S\) for the second derivative of the penalty, $$V_b = (H + S)^{-1}, \qquad V_f = (H+S)^{-1} H (H+S)^{-1}.$$ \(V_b\) is the posterior variance under the prior whose negative logarithm is the penalty, and it is the matrix from which an interval around a penalized term should be built: it carries the smoothing bias as variance, and for that reason such intervals cover at about their nominal rate. \(V_f\) is the sampling variance of the penalized estimator at a fixed penalty, which is smaller and covers less. With no penalty \(S = 0\) and both are \(H^{-1}\), for a coefficient that the outer criterion does not estimate. Under reml() or ml() with the default marginal = NULL, in a model without a structural term, the unpenalized coefficients of every distribution parameter other than the first (for example the log standard deviation of a Gaussian) are estimated on the criterion, and "bayesian" and "unconditional" take the curvature of that criterion for them. These two types then differ from "frequentist" for those coefficients even without a penalty.

For a prior that is not Gaussian, \(V_b\) is computed in the same way for every penalty that is twice differentiable at the mode. \(H + S\) is then the curvature of the log-posterior at the mode, and \(V_b\) is the Laplace approximation of the posterior variance. The statement about coverage above holds for a Gaussian prior, whose \(S\) does not depend on the coefficients. For another prior \(S\) is evaluated at the estimate and can be negative. Under a Student t prior with scale \(s\) and \(\nu\) degrees of freedom it is negative for every effect larger than \(\sqrt{\nu}\, s\) in absolute value, so such an effect is shrunk little and its variance comes mostly from the likelihood. The approximation is local, and it can be poor where the posterior is skewed or has more than one mode. Where \(H + S\) is not positive definite, a coordinate whose diagonal entry is not positive is held as described below, and otherwise an error is signaled.

The first two matrices are conditional on the hyperparameters, which are evaluated at the value where the outer search stopped, as though that value were known. It was estimated from the same data, and the third matrix adds the variance that this estimation contributes: $$V' = V_b + J V_\theta J', \qquad J = -(H + S)^{-1} \frac{\partial^2 \rho}{\partial\beta \partial\theta},$$ with \(V_\theta\) the variance of the estimated hyperparameters on their own free scale. It is the delta method applied to the map from the hyperparameter to the penalized mode (Wood, Pya and Safken, 2016), and the matrix that mgcv returns as unconditional = TRUE. The correction is positive semi-definite, so \(V'\) is never narrower than \(V_b\). It matters where a smoothing parameter is poorly determined, and it affects the penalized coordinates much more than the unpenalized ones. It requires the curvature of the outer criterion, which the two conditional matrices do not read, so "unconditional" is more expensive than the other two types.

Where no hyperparameter was estimated by a differentiable criterion there is nothing to propagate, the correction is exactly zero and "unconditional" returns \(V_b\) itself. Where a hyperparameter was estimated and the curvature of the criterion cannot be read at the fitted point, the conditional matrix is returned with a warning, so that the narrower matrix is not mistaken for the wider one. Where the curvature can be read for only some of the hyperparameters, the correction is a lower bound and a warning states it. See hyper_correction().

A coefficient that a kinked penalty has set to zero has NA in its row and column. At zero the penalty is not twice differentiable, so \(S\) does not exist there and the curvature cannot be read. The coefficients that a lasso or an MCP leaves non-zero have a variance, which is conditional on that selection; summary.StatmodFit() reports this in a note. Away from zero the lasso contributes nothing to \(S\), and SCAD and MCP contribute a negative curvature on their concave part, which makes the variance of a coefficient there larger than that of the likelihood alone. For these penalties \(V_b\) is therefore not the posterior variance under the corresponding prior, because a curvature read at the mode does not include the mass that the prior puts near zero.

The argument expected selects the matrix used as \(H\). Its default is the expected information where the fit inverted it and the family writes it out in closed form, and the observed Hessian otherwise (fit_expected()). The two agree asymptotically and not in a sample: one is the information averaged over the model, and the other is the curvature of the likelihood at the data in hand. A model that carries a structural term is always inverted on the observed information, because a filter and a mixture over states do not have an expected information.

Where the family has no closed form, expected = TRUE reaches an approximation, and approx selects it. "opg", the default, is the outer product of the observed scores and costs one gradient; "bartlett" evaluates the expectation itself, a sum over the support for a discrete family and a quadrature for a continuous one, and is orders of magnitude more expensive. The expensive route is available and is not the default.

References

Wood, S. N., Pya, N. and Safken, B. (2016). Smoothing parameter and model selection for general smooth models. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 111(516), 1548–1563.

See also

confint.StatmodFit(), summary.StatmodFit(), hyper_correction(), which builds the third matrix's correction

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(80))
dd$y <- 1 + 2 * dd$x + rnorm(80, sd = 0.4)
fit <- statmod(y ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd)
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))
#>    mu:(Intercept)              mu:x sigma:(Intercept) 
#>        0.08770104        0.14865515        0.08006408 

# With a penalized term the three differ for a penalized coefficient, and
# the widest is the one that does not read the smoothing parameter as known.
ds <- data.frame(x = runif(200))
ds$y <- sin(2 * pi * ds$x) + rnorm(200, sd = 0.3)
fs <- statmod(y ~ s(x, bspline_smooth(k = 10)), distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), ds)
vapply(c("frequentist", "bayesian", "unconditional"),
       function(ty) sqrt(diag(vcov(fs, type = ty)))[["mu:s(x).z2"]], 0)
#>   frequentist      bayesian unconditional 
#>    0.06507969    0.06551107    0.06623606
